Foods & recipes

Food database

—

AUSNUT 2023 (FSANZ) is built in whole — 3,741 foods, straight from the official nutrient profiles, including the composite dishes and commercial products the national survey actually recorded. The 386 foods from Food Composition Database Release 3 that AUSNUT has no entry for are carried over, so nothing is lost. Solids are per 100 g; the 348 foods FSANZ measures by volume are per 100 mL, which is the honest basis for a drink. Energy is the label figure, calculated with dietary fibre. Household portions come from FSANZ's own measures file wherever it has them.

Supermarket products

FSANZ covers named products where the survey met them, not the whole branded shelf at Coles. For the rest, Open Food Facts is the open, barcode-level database — filter it by brand or country on their advanced search, download the result as CSV, and load it here. Tab-separated exports, sodium in grams and salt-only rows are all handled.

It is crowd-sourced, so coverage is patchy and the odd entry is wrong — imports stay under their own Packaged category so you always know which numbers came from FSANZ and which did not. For a single item, the panel on the box beats any database: use New food.

Product data from Open Food Facts, used under the Open Database License. Their API allows about ten searches a minute per person, so lookups are deliberately one tap at a time rather than as you type.

Off by default. Switched on, the search sheet offers a button to query Open Food Facts for whatever you typed — one request, on your tap, carrying the search text and nothing else. No account, no identifier, no history. Anything you pick is saved to this device so it works offline afterwards.
